note: SBA borrowing principle: borrow composition, concepts and ways of thinking about materials — never copy the style.

same: Both focus on people's isolation in city life
Both start from everyday spaces (restaurants, homes)
diff: Edward Hopper (霍普) uses realist oil painting and strong light and shadow; Pak Sheung-chuen (白雙全) uses conceptual art and ready-mades
Hopper depicts scenes; Pak measures and materialises space itself
sba: Borrow Hopper's window-frame / glass divisions in your composition to show the distance between people
Borrow Pak's concept of 'collecting invisible things' to turn the cramped pressure of subdivided flats and classrooms into visible objects

same: Both use natural scenery to carry inner states
The brushstrokes / ink marks themselves are traces of emotion
diff: Vincent van Gogh (梵高) uses high saturation and swirling impasto; Lui Shou-kwan (呂壽琨) uses blocks of dry, dark ink and blank space
Van Gogh's emotions burst outward; Lui leans towards Zen-like introspection
sba: Borrow Van Gogh's 'brushstroke direction expresses emotion', using line rhythm to record how your mood changes over a day
Borrow Lui's blank space to give the picture room to breathe, expressing calm or detachment

same: Both give up recognisable images and use colour to create a spiritual space
Both aim for an immersive emotional experience for the viewer
diff: Mark Rothko (羅斯科) uses large soft-edged colour blocks in a still structure; Zao Wou-Ki (趙無極) brings in calligraphic brush movement, so his pictures flow
Zao is rooted in Chinese landscape painting and calligraphy; Rothko comes from Western colour field painting
sba: Borrow Rothko's layered colour blocks, using two or three colours to express one emotion
Borrow Zao's brush movement, turning calligraphic gestures into an abstract composition

same: Both appropriate familiar popular images and commercial brands
Both use the visual language of mass production, such as flat colour and repetition
diff: Andy Warhol (沃荷) shows the surface of American consumer culture and celebrity worship
Wang Guangyi (王廣義) places political propaganda posters next to Western brands, with an ironic edge
sba: Borrow repeated arrangement (a screen-print effect) to explore the brands or social media images in students' daily lives
Borrow the idea of 'juxtaposing two image systems' to create critical meaning

same: Both explore identity through images of people
Both use symbolic objects to tell stories
diff: Frida Kahlo (卡蘿) uses self-portraits to confront bodily pain and Mexican culture
Wilson Shieh (石家豪) uses gongbi fine brushwork in rich colour and faceless figures to explore Hong Kong identity and gender roles
sba: Borrow Kahlo's 'self-portrait + symbolic objects', using things around you to express your own identity
Borrow Shieh's Chinese gongbi technique with contemporary subjects to create a dialogue between tradition and the present

same: Both break everyday logic to create a dreamlike feeling
Both have humour and poetry
diff: René Magritte (馬格利特) paints impossible scenes in a calm, realist manner
Luis Chan (陳福善) uses bright colours and naïve forms, with a sense of fantasy and folk humour
sba: Borrow Magritte's 'displacement', putting familiar objects into illogical scenes
Borrow Luis Chan's free use of colour to turn Hong Kong street scenes into a fantasy world

same: Both make the installation / experience of space the artwork itself
Both make viewers notice perceptions they usually overlook
diff: Olafur Eliasson (埃利亞松) uses natural phenomena such as light, water and mist, on a grand scale
Lee Kit (李傑) uses canvas, projection and everyday objects, with a quiet, intimate mood
sba: Borrow Eliasson's use of light to change how a space feels, and make a small light installation
Borrow the mood of Lee Kit's 'small everyday moments' to record your home space

same: Both explore close relationships through portraits / group portraits
Both deliberately flatten the picture
diff: David Hockney (霍克尼) uses bright colours to show life and friends in California
Zhang Xiaogang (張曉剛) uses grey tones and 'bloodline' threads to evoke collective memory and a sense of repression
sba: Borrow Hockney's double-portrait compositions to analyse distance and relationships between figures
Borrow Zhang Xiaogang's 'old photos + thin connecting lines' to show family memory

same: Both seek order and balance in the picture
Both use lines to divide space
diff: Piet Mondrian (蒙德里安) uses vertical and horizontal lines and primary colours: pure geometry
Wucius Wong (王無邪) combines design principles with Chinese landscape, so geometry and ink coexist
sba: Borrow Mondrian's grid divisions to show city planning or a timetable
Borrow Wucius Wong's way of placing design elements in landscape to create an East–West fusion composition

same: Both explore states of existence through sculptures of the human body
Both use 'missing' parts to spark the imagination
diff: Alberto Giacometti (賈柯梅蒂) stretches and thins the body to express existentialist loneliness
Bruno Catalano (卡塔拉諾) hollows out the body to express the loss felt by travellers and migrants
sba: Borrow Giacometti's exaggerated proportions to express a psychological state
Borrow Catalano's 'missing parts' to express diaspora or things lost while growing up

same: Both build form on drawing and the anatomy of people or animals
Both treat careful observation as the root of art
diff: Leonardo da Vinci uses oil sfumato for soft volume; Xu Beihong (徐悲鴻) puts drawing structure into ink brushwork
Leonardo seeks scientific understanding; Xu's galloping horses carry national spirit
sba: Borrow their anatomy-sketch method: draw bones and muscles first, then add colour
Borrow Xu's idea of drawing structure in ink to try showing volume with ink

same: Both make ordinary people the main characters
Both use realist oil painting to show real human nature
diff: Caravaggio uses dark backgrounds and spotlight contrast for drama; Liu Xiaodong (劉小東) paints on site in natural light
Caravaggio casts ordinary people in religious stories; Liu records present-day social life directly
sba: Borrow Caravaggio's single strong light: photograph people you know and study light and dark
Borrow Liu's on-site painting: draw real people at a market or station

same: Both value the feeling of colour and light over detail
Both often take landscape and nature as subjects
diff: Claude Monet paints outdoors with short broken oil strokes; Lin Fengmian (林風眠) uses ink and colour on rice paper in square formats
Monet records a moment of light; Lin blends in folk art for a lyrical mood
sba: Borrow Monet's series: paint one place at three different times of day
Borrow Lin's square format: crop a landscape into a square and organise it with colour blocks

same: Both mastered traditional skills before breaking away boldly
Both developed new styles in their later work
diff: Pablo Picasso breaks objects into geometry and many viewpoints; Zhang Daqian (張大千) breaks outlines with splashed ink and colour
Picasso moves toward Cubist space; Zhang moves toward semi-abstract landscape mood
sba: Borrow Picasso's many viewpoints: combine the front and side of one object in a single picture
Borrow Zhang's splashed colour: let paint flow freely first, then add a few fine details

same: Both express life with very simple shapes and clear colours
Both have a light, childlike sense of fun
diff: Henri Matisse uses flat colour and paper cut-outs; Qi Baishi (齊白石) uses ink brushwork with red flowers and ink leaves
Matisse seeks harmony of colour; Qi values lively brushwork
sba: Borrow Matisse's cut-outs: cut your subject into simple colour shapes and arrange them
Borrow Qi's economy: paint a small animal in as few strokes as possible

same: Both depict dream scenes that break real-world logic
Both use fine technique to make the absurd believable
diff: Salvador Dalí uses oil paint and melting objects; Joey Leung Ka-yin (梁嘉賢) uses fine lines and humorous text
Dalí explores unsettling subconscious; Leung shows a light, humorous personal world
sba: Borrow Dalí's distortion: "melt" an everyday object or change its texture
Borrow Leung's text plus image: add your own caption to a dream scene

pairs.theme: Point, line, plane and formal beauty
same: Both make points, lines, planes and colour the stars of the picture
Both believe form itself can carry feeling and rhythm
diff: Wassily Kandinsky goes fully abstract; Wu Guanzhong (吳冠中) keeps scenes such as Jiangnan villages
Kandinsky uses oil and musical analogies; Wu uses ink lines and black, white and grey
sba: Borrow Kandinsky: turn the rhythm of a song into dots and lines
Borrow Wu: simplify a street photo into black, white and grey planes with colour dots

same: Both take flowers as a main subject
Both start from close observation of nature
diff: Georgia O'Keeffe enlarges a flower to fill the canvas; Chao Shao-an (趙少昂) places flowers, birds and insects in empty space
O'Keeffe uses soft gradients in oil; Chao uses lively brushwork
sba: Borrow O'Keeffe's close-up: enlarge a flower until you cannot see all of it
Borrow Chao's empty space: use a few strokes with lots of blank paper

same: Both make simplified, rounded human forms
Both respect the texture of the material
diff: Henry Moore uses stone and bronze with pierced holes; Wang Keping (王克平) carves wood and keeps the grain and knots
Moore explores form and space; Wang also responds to social oppression
sba: Borrow Moore's voids: cut a hole through a clay model so space becomes part of it
Borrow Wang: let the original shape of a block of wood or stone decide the pose

same: Both use distorted or exaggerated figures to show inner unease
Both use expressionist brushwork
diff: Francis Bacon blurs and twists faces inside cage-like frames; Zeng Fanzhi (曾梵志) hides real expressions behind white masks
Bacon expresses post-war existential anxiety; Zeng shows disguise in relationships
sba: Borrow Bacon's frames: use lines to "trap" a figure in the middle of the picture
Borrow Zeng's mask: add a mask to your self-portrait for the face you show others

same: Both make the painter's gesture the main subject
Both are abstract painters
diff: Jackson Pollock drips paint on canvas on the floor in an all-over composition; Chu Teh-Chun (朱德群) builds layers of light with calligraphic strokes
Pollock stresses chance; Chu keeps a sense of landscape
sba: Borrow Pollock: drip paint on a large sheet using your whole body and record the rhythm
Borrow Chu: write one character with a big brush, then develop it into abstract light

same: Both use ideas to challenge what viewers think "art" or "writing" is
Both make viewers question habits they take for granted
diff: Marcel Duchamp chooses ready-mades with no handcraft; Xu Bing (徐冰) spends huge effort carving fake characters
Duchamp questions the definition of art; Xu questions language and culture
sba: Borrow Duchamp: pick an everyday object and give it a new title that changes its meaning
Borrow Xu: invent your own script and write a sentence only you can read

same: Both respond to social and political issues
Both make clever use of media and public attention
diff: Banksy sprays walls anonymously; Ai Weiwei (艾未未) works openly with large installations and documentaries
Banksy uses dark humour; Ai uses masses of repeated objects
sba: Borrow Banksy: design a stencil image with one clear social message
Borrow Ai: build an issue out of many identical small objects

same: Both build works from one mark repeated many times
Both create strong rhythm through repetition
diff: Yayoi Kusama uses dots and mirror rooms tied to personal psychology; Ding Yi (丁乙) uses grids of crosses with rational order
Kusama seeks "self-obliteration"; Ding responds to industrial and urban rhythm
sba: Borrow Kusama: cover a whole object in one mark and see how it "disappears"
Borrow Ding: arrange two marks on grid paper to make a changing pattern

same: Both borrow the language of film
Both explore how images shape identity
diff: Cindy Sherman poses as characters in made-up film stills; Chow Chun Fai (周俊輝) repaints real Hong Kong film scenes with subtitles
Sherman looks at images of women; Chow looks at Hong Kong identity
sba: Borrow Sherman: create a character and shoot your own "film still"
Borrow Chow: repaint a film frame and add your own subtitle

same: Both use video to handle time and pace
Both seek cinematic, poetic images
diff: Bill Viola uses extreme slow motion about life, death and faith; Yang Fudong (楊福東) uses black-and-white narrative about lost youth
Viola often uses one large projection; Yang often uses multiple screens and long stories
sba: Borrow Viola: film one simple action in slow motion
Borrow Yang: film classmates' daily moments in black and white

same: Both use their own bodies as the medium
Both test limits through long or harsh actions
diff: Marina Abramović focuses on contact with the audience; Zhang Huan (張洹) focuses on the body in its environment
Abramović often performs in museums; Zhang's early work happened in everyday places and was documented in photos
sba: Borrow from both: photograph how a repeated action changes over time
Only do safe performance exercises; focus on recording the process, not on suffering

same: Both use mirror-polished stainless steel
Both make the surroundings and viewers' reflections part of the work
diff: Anish Kapoor uses abstract curves to explore space and void; Zhan Wang (展望) copies the shape of traditional garden rocks
Kapoor focuses on perception; Zhan reflects on tradition and modernisation
sba: Borrow from both: wrap an object in foil or mirror paper and photograph what it reflects
Borrow Zhan: remake a traditional object in an industrial material

same: Both deal with race and history
Both surround viewers with large installations
diff: Kara Walker uses black silhouettes to expose violent history; Gu Wenda (谷文達) uses hair from many countries to express cultural fusion
Walker's tone is sharp; Gu leans toward an ideal of unity
sba: Borrow Walker: tell a story about history in silhouettes
Borrow Gu: collect one material from many people to represent a group

same: Both draw on youth subcultures such as anime and games
Both blur art and popular culture
diff: Takashi Murakami uses flat painting and cute characters; Cao Fei (曹斐) uses video and virtual game worlds
Murakami embraces commercial projects; Cao looks at urban youth alienation
sba: Borrow Murakami: design yourself as a "Superflat" character
Borrow Cao: use game or virtual-world screenshots to discuss a real city problem

same: Both enlarge familiar symbols into sculpture
Both change a symbol's meaning through scale and material
diff: Jeff Koons uses shiny steel for consumer kitsch; Sui Jianguo (隋建國) uses empty Mao suits to reflect on history
Koons feels playful and celebratory; Sui carries heavy memory
sba: Borrow Koons: remake a cheap toy in a "precious" material
Borrow Sui: choose a garment that stands for an era and make it as an empty shell

same: Both use specimen-style display to explore life and death
Both borrow the look of science and museums
diff: Damien Hirst preserves real animals in formaldehyde; Shen Shaomin (沈少民) assembles imaginary creatures from bones
Hirst also raises issues of commerce and the market; Shen focuses on survival and evolution
sba: Borrow from both: write a museum-style label for an object you invent
Assemble an imaginary creature from leaves, shells and other natural materials

same: Both care about balance in composition
Both create tension with simple shapes and colours
diff: Alexander Calder balances hanging metal shapes in real space; Pan Tianshou (潘天壽) balances big rocks and hard lines on a flat surface
Calder's works move; Pan freezes tension by creating then resolving visual risk
sba: Borrow Calder: build a balancing mobile from wire and card
Borrow Pan: put the main subject near the edge, then balance it with another element

same: Both render skin and wrinkles in extreme detail
Both use huge scale for psychological impact
diff: Ron Mueck works in 3D and may enlarge or shrink; Luo Zhongli (羅中立) paints a giant flat portrait
Mueck looks at universal emotions; Luo looks at the hard life of farmers
sba: Borrow from both: draw an ordinary face much larger than life
Borrow Mueck: make a figure much smaller than life and notice how the feeling changes

same: Both value the raw texture of materials (concrete, plywood)
Both think about people and nature
diff: Tadao Ando brings real light and nature into built space; Lam Tung Pang (林東鵬) paints remembered landscapes on plywood
Ando seeks calm; Lam carries the city's collective memory
sba: Borrow Ando: make a small card model where light enters through a slit
Borrow Lam: paint on a textured material and let its grain become part of the picture

same: Both use photography to criticise consumerism
Both borrow the visual language of advertising
diff: Barbara Kruger pairs black-and-white photos with white-on-red slogans; Wang Qingsong (王慶松) stages large, exaggerated scenes
Kruger speaks to the viewer directly; Wang satirises society through theatre-like scenes
sba: Borrow Kruger: add a slogan questioning consumption to an advert photo
Borrow Wang: stage an exaggerated shopping scene with classmates

same: Both use real personal belongings
Both make private stories public so others can relate
diff: Tracey Emin focuses on personal feelings and trauma; Song Dong (宋冬) focuses on family history and memories of scarcity
Emin adds neon and embroidery; Song lays out masses of objects in order
sba: Borrow Emin: pair a handwritten line with one personal object
Borrow Song: lay out one type of old household object neatly and photograph it

same: Both use animals or hybrid creatures to raise ethical questions
Both make viewers feel drawn in and uneasy at once
diff: Patricia Piccinini makes lifelike silicone imaginary creatures; Huang Yong Ping (黃永砅) used real insects and animals
Piccinini looks at biotechnology; Huang looked at culture clashes and power
sba: Borrow Piccinini: design a creature mixing two animals and describe its "purpose"
Borrow Huang: use animals as a metaphor for two cultures meeting

same: Both create huge, short-lived outdoor events
Both extend the work through photos and records
diff: Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrap landmarks in fabric; Cai Guo-Qiang (蔡國強) uses the instant of a gunpowder explosion
Wrappings last weeks; explosions last seconds
sba: Borrow Christo: wrap an object on campus in cloth or paper and photograph it
Borrow Cai: safely record the trace of an instant (e.g. dripped ink, sprayed water)

same: Both play on the gap between a first glance and a closer look
Both surround viewers with immersive installations
diff: Leandro Erlich uses mirrors and buildings for spatial illusions; Tsang Kin-Wah (曾建華) hides sharp words in floral patterns
Erlich leans toward play and participation; Tsang toward religion and existence
sba: Borrow Erlich: use a mirror to take an "impossible" photo
Borrow Tsang: arrange words into a pattern that means something different up close

same: Both respond to alienation brought by modernisation
Both use industrial or urban found materials
diff: Ashley Bickerton makes object-like works with logos; Big Tail Elephants (大尾象工作組) used temporary spaces and performance
Bickerton looks at people, nature and technology; Big Tail looked at rapid urbanisation in Guangdong
sba: Borrow Bickerton: put brand logos on natural objects and see what tension appears
Borrow Big Tail: hold a pop-up display in a non-gallery school space such as a stairwell

same: Both brought Western art into China in the early 20th century
Both were pioneers from Guangdong
diff: Li Tiefu adopted Western classical oil painting directly; Gao Jianfu (高劍父) reformed Chinese painting with Western methods
Li focused on realist portraits; Gao on modern subjects and brushwork
sba: Compare them: paint one subject with a Western medium, then by adapting a local medium
Borrow Gao: put a modern object into a traditional ink composition

same: Both belong to the Lingnan School and excel at birds and animals
Both work from life sketching
diff: Gao Qifeng's animals are powerful; Yang Shen-sum's (楊善深) brushwork is more fluid
Gao is first-generation; Yang is second-generation and lived in Hong Kong
sba: Sketch an animal at a park or pet shop, then paint it once "forceful" and once "flowing"
Compare how each brush style changes the animal's character

same: Both stress sketching real scenery from life
Both belong to the Lingnan School
diff: Chen Shuren is fresh and light; Guan Shanyue (關山月) is grand with rich colour
Chen favours small poetic scenes; Guan large mountains and rivers
sba: At one spot, paint a small close-up and a wide panorama
Compare how light and rich colour change the mood

pairs.theme: Personal voices in Hong Kong ink
same: Both hold important places in Hong Kong ink painting
Both turned traditional brushwork into a personal style
diff: Au Ho-nien works from life with strong colour; Fang Zhaoling (方召麐) uses bold calligraphic lines and childlike forms
Au continues the Lingnan tradition; Fang is closer to calligraphic expression
sba: Borrow Fang: paint a mountain as if writing calligraphy
Borrow Au: add strong colour after sketching from life

same: Both are leading 1990s Cynical Realists
Both repeat a figure type to express the mood of the time
diff: Yue Minjun uses exaggerated laughter; Fang Lijun (方力鈞) uses bald heads and yawns
Yue's colour is loud and bright; Fang often uses sky and water backgrounds
sba: Design one repeated expression for your generation's mood
Compare how "laughing" and "bored" can express the same loss

same: Both work with new media (video, sound)
Both use time-based media
diff: Zhang Peili uses repeated actions and a cool camera; Samson Young (楊嘉輝) uses soundscapes and performance
Zhang looks at daily life and surveillance; Young at politics and history
sba: Borrow Zhang: film one repeated action for ten minutes with a fixed camera
Borrow Young: record school sounds and make a "sound map"

same: Both were members of Big Tail Elephants
Both take Pearl River Delta cities such as Guangzhou as their subject
diff: Chen Shaoxiong uses ink animation and street collage; Xu Tan (徐坦) uses interviews and keyword research
Chen leans visual; Xu leans verbal
sba: Borrow Chen: trace street photos in ink and make a simple animation
Borrow Xu: interview ten people to find your neighbourhood's keywords

same: Both use text as their main material
Both are Chinese conceptual artists
diff: Wu Shanzhuan uses slogan-like text and absurd acts to challenge institutions; Qiu Zhijie (邱志杰) uses repeated writing and concept maps to organise knowledge
Wu leans toward satire; Qiu toward thinking and systems
sba: Borrow Qiu: draw a concept map for your SBA theme
Borrow Wu: fill a wall with slogan-like text and watch how meaning shifts

same: Both create with old and found objects
Both explore family and social memory
diff: Yin Xiuzhen sews used clothes into soft sculpture; Tang Kwok Hin (鄧國騫) collages found objects
Yin links to global identity; Tang to Hong Kong family and social space
sba: Borrow Yin: sew a small work from family members' old clothes
Borrow Tang: collage a "home" map from household objects
